sentences.text: The first two weeks were frustrating for Ilona.
Uncle Béla was patient but firm.
Every day at four o'clock they sat at the kitchen table, and he opened jars, and he made her taste them, and he asked her what she tasted.
At first she could only say "honey." He would nod and let her try again.
Slowly she started to notice things.
Bitter.
Sweet.
Floral.
Pepper.
Woody.
She began to have words for the differences.
But even when she could describe a taste, she could not connect the taste to a place.
Uncle Béla would say, "So where were the bees?
Look at the map.
Where were they in mid-July?" And she would guess wrong.
She did not know what acacia tasted like, or thyme, or clover.
She was a city child.
She was learning a language that she had no vocabulary for.
It felt impossible.
On the tenth day she got angry and pushed her jar away and said, "Uncle Béla, I can't do this.
Nobody does this anymore.
Why does it matter."
Uncle Béla did not answer right away.
He took the jar back.
He put the lid on it.
He did not look angry, but he did not look happy either.
He said, quietly, "It matters because when I die, this will die.
My father was the last one who knew this.
His mother taught him.
I have been trying for years to find someone to teach it to.
Everyone says nobody does this anymore.
Everyone says it is silly.
But when the last person who can do it is gone, then it is gone.
That is what a lost thing is."
Ilona sat with her hands in her lap.
She had not thought of it like that.
She said, "I'm sorry." Uncle Béla shook his head.
"Do not be sorry.
But do not stop.
It is your choice, of course.
You can go home whenever you want.
But if you stay, please be serious about it.
If you do it you might be the last one after me.
Or you might not.
Maybe you teach it to your own daughter someday.
That is what I hope for.
But even if you never teach anyone, you will know.
That is enough.
Someone will still know how to read a jar of honey."
So Ilona kept trying.
After that day, Uncle Béla changed how he taught her.
Instead of tasting inside, he took her out onto the hills.
He showed her the acacia trees, and he had her taste an acacia flower.
"See?
Slightly sweet, slightly like grass.
This is what the honey will taste like." He showed her the thyme, and had her rub it between her fingers, and smell it.
He showed her wild sunflowers, and buckwheat fields, and a small stand of lime trees behind the church.
Each thing had a smell and a taste, and each thing translated, later, into a taste in the honey.
It was slow going.
But it was better than the kitchen.
Ilona began to like the walks.
She began to like the plants.
She began to like Uncle Béla in a new way — not just as the great-uncle who used to give her honey on toast, but as a person who knew things.
Real things.
Things that were hard to know.
By the end of the third week, Ilona could get some things right.
Not everything.
Not most things.
But sometimes.
Uncle Béla would open a jar, and she would taste it with her eyes closed, and she would say, "This is acacia.
Early.
Maybe the third week of June." And Uncle Béla would smile and check the label, and she would be right.
When she was right, she felt something completely new.
It was not exactly pride.
It was more like — recognition.
As if she had opened a door and found a room that had always been there, waiting.
"You are doing it," he said, one evening.
"You are actually doing it.
I did not know if you would.
I thought maybe you would not.
But you are."
"Uncle Béla," she said.
"There are seven jars in a row.
I know what six of them are.
But there is one from last week that I cannot figure out.
It has something in it I have not tasted before." Uncle Béla nodded.
"Bring it out." She got up and got it from the shelf.
It was the last jar of the season, from the very last collection Uncle Béla had done, three days before Ilona had first come.
It was a light amber color, unremarkable to look at.
She poured a small spoonful onto her spoon.
She tasted it again.
There it was.
Something she could not name.
Something that reminded her of somewhere, but she did not know where.
